question: Xi Jinping out before 2027?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if China's General Secretary of the Communist Party, Xi Jinping, is removed from power for any length of time between July 3, 2025, and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping will be considered removed from power if he announces his resignation from his role as General Secretary, or is otherwise dismissed, detained, disqualified, or otherwise loses his position or is prevented from fulfilling his duties as General Secretary within this market's timeframe.

The primary resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.

eventMetadata.context_description: Xi Jinping's consolidated control over the Chinese Communist Party's central institutions, including the Politburo and Central Committee, underpins the 95% trader consensus against his removal before 2027. With no designated successor or formal age-based retirement pressure applying to him, and the 21st Party Congress slated for late 2027 as the next major leadership forum, recent analyses show expectations of continuity into a fourth term rather than abrupt change. Military purges and elite reshuffles have further aligned top ranks without evident challenges to his authority. While improbable, scenarios such as a sudden health crisis, major undisclosed scandal, or unprecedented internal factional realignment could still shift outcomes before year-end 2026.

The resolution source for this market will be a consensus of official Democratic Party sources.

Any replacement of the democratic nominee before election day will not change the resolution of the market.

eventMetadata.context_description: The Democratic presidential nomination race for 2028 remains wide open more than two years before primaries, with trader consensus reflected in fragmented pricing across a large field of potential contenders. The DNC’s August 2026 revision of the primary calendar—starting in South Carolina and sequencing through Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, and Virginia—has boosted candidates positioned for early support in diverse and battleground electorates. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez leads implied probabilities after recent statements indicating she has not ruled out a bid, alongside gains in early-state polling, while Jon Ossoff draws visibility from his Senate role and Georgia reelection cycle and Gavin Newsom leverages executive experience in the largest state. Kamala Harris retains name recognition but trails current market levels, and the absence of formal announcements or major endorsements keeps probabilities tightly clustered. Developments such as 2026 midterm outcomes, candidate entries, and shifts in national or state polling could quickly create separation among the top contenders.
